doc.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Making seven stereo LPs for Decca, moving to Connecticut
summary: Dance recorded mainstream LPs at Victor in early stereo, made the Hodges album under another name, produced Dickie Wells and Earl Hines sessions, and moved to Connecticut.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: And you said they were LPs? They weren’t ten inch records? They were —

But that was just when stereo was coming in. And these engineers were full of jargon, and it didn’t mean a thing to me, I just wanted a good monaural record. So the mainstream thing was a good, commercial slogan. That gave them something new to talk about.

But the records did reasonably well. There was beginners luck in part too, because some, where my heart was really in, didn’t come out so well, but others came out very well. So I go back and these are issued in Europe, with quite good reviews etcetera. And the following year, my wife never really got used to the English climate, and then we were living in a house that was 400 years old you know. And of course the property after World War II in England was at a premium. My father’s house opposite where we lived was 500 years old. But I was accustomed to that. So we decided to move to Connecticut where her father had a place. And he offered us a house sort of rent free. And I thought my wife and I can start up again. For Decca, I had to make I think it was two more albums for Decca. And I’d previously made one with Dickie Wells, the trombone player, and three other trombones, four trombones and a rhythm section, which was unusual but was successful and I made a number of those. And the other one I was counting on to do when Duke’s manager came to me one day and said, “I hear you’re making some more records.” I said yes. “Then why not use my guys — our guys.” I said, “Oh Duke doesn’t want that.” He said, “Yeah, those guys need the money.” So I said, “Well can I have Johnny Hodges?” He says, “Yeah, you can have Johnny Hodges, you can just give him another name.” And so I knew I couldn’t have Duke, you know, so Billy Strayhorn could play piano. And that’s how that album came about, which is rather a fixed subject in — I don’t know whether you’ve read Hasse’s book, well you know it’s completely misinterpreted, it’s as though I was trying to pull a fast one because I knew exactly that Johnny Hodges was a close friend of mine and I knew very well that he was under contract to Norman Granz you know. And then that was the end of Decca and those two. And then in the first batch, one of the things that led to more activity was Earl Hines, another of my idols. He was in San Francisco and I hadn’t the time or the money to go out there, but a Belgian friend of mind was going out and I got him to record a session, which was very successful. And then after a time I had an English friend who was recording, called Dennis Preston, he made quite a few records for him which were issued on English Columbia. And I started to write. I wrote for various jazz magazines — when I had a year when I was the jazz critic of the New York Herald Tribune, which was bad, that was a terrible job really.
